The dispute is a route_deviation complaint by the rider, on a RydeX trip (fixed quote, estimate 9.9 km, charged $23.32) [F1][F4][F6]. There is exactly one off-route segment: 10:04–10:07, 1.94 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.22 km, adding 1.73 km, up to 947 m from the optimal route [F3]. Under RD-1 that segment is a detour unless RD-3, RD-4 or RD-5 excuses it.

RD-5 decides the segment. The driver proposed the change before leaving the optimal route — Chat #1 at 10:01: "Traffic ahead on Tampines Expressway is building up, ok if I go round via Halus Link?" [F7] — and the rider agreed at 10:01: "Sure, go ahead" [F8]. The agreement timestamp precedes the segment's start at 10:04 [F3][F8], which is precisely the RD-5 pattern (agreement before the detour). The driver named the route ("via Halus Link") before leaving, so the consent covers that named corridor; consent scope is not stretched beyond the named route, and this segment plainly lies on the named Halus Link routing rather than somewhere else. RD-5 therefore exempts F3, and RD-3 does not apply because there was no rider-requested stop [F3][F7][F8][RD-5][RD-3].

RD-4 does not exempt the segment and is not needed. The only traffic records are Tampines Expressway and Punggol Road at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) covering 09:49–10:21 [F10][F11], and no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window [F12]. Band 4 is neither a DataMall incident under RD-4(a) nor a band 1/2 record, and RD-4(b) never exempts a segment on its own [F10][F11][F12][RD-4]. The driver's account of building congestion [F9] cannot substitute for the evidence RD-4 requires — but the segment is already exempt under RD-5, so no unexempted segment remains under RD-1 [F3][F9][RD-1][RD-4][RD-5].

With no unexempted segment, RD-2's refund formula has nothing to operate on. In any event this is a non-metered RydeX trip: the billed distance equals the optimal distance (9.9 km) [F4], there is no surge (1.0×) [F5], and the $23.32 total decomposes entirely into published components — base $3.90, distance $14.02, time $3.93, waiting $0.00, platform $1.47, discount $0.00 — with no ERP/toll item and no manually added charge [F6]. Refundable amount = $0.00, so the outcome is no_action with the driver's shortest-route duty not breached on these facts [F4][F5][F6][RD-2][FARE-1].

RD-6 is not triggered: an account flag requires the case to be made out against the driver (refund > 0 or a recorded RD-1 breach) plus route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1 [F15], and here there is neither a refund nor an unexempted segment, and the driver's single upheld dispute in 90 days is not a route dispute [F3][F6][F15][RD-6]. Profile facts (rider's 2 disputes / 0 upheld; driver's record) do not decide the case [F14][F15].

DRIVER: We looked into the rider's route complaint and are closing it with no action against you.

What decided it: before you left the usual route, you messaged the rider asking to go around via Halus Link due to traffic, and the rider agreed. Because the agreement came first, the extra distance is treated as approved and no refund arises.

The ride was a fixed-quote RydeX fare of $23.32, so there is no refundable amount. Your driver account is not affected and no action is being taken against you.

claims.assertion: The driver deviated from the shortest and most direct route: the GPS track shows one off-route segment (10:04–10:07) driving 1.94 km where the optimal route covers 0.22 km, i.e. 1.73 km of extra distance, up to 947 m away from the optimal route.

The deviation was not justified by traffic: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, and the only speed-band records on the optimal route were band 4 (30–39 km/h), which is neither a DataMall incident nor a band 1/2 congestion record, so RD-4 gives the driver no exemption.

The rider's consent in chat #2 (10:01) was given before the off-route segment began (10:04), so the driver did ask in advance and the rider did agree to the Halus Link route; this consent cannot be used against the rider but also means the rider shared the routing choice.

This trip is a RydeX (non-metered, fixed-fare) service: the fare was quoted at booking and the driver billed exactly the optimal distance (9.9 km), with no distance excess, no waiting fee and no undisclosed add-on, so the rider's money was not increased by the extra 1.8 km actually driven.

Because no additional charge entered the fare, there is nothing to refund under RD-2's non-metered branch — the refundable amount is $0 (computed from the billed fare in F6, which contains no off-route ERP/toll or manually added item), so the correct monetary outcome is no_action while the driver's breach of the shortest-route duty is recorded.
The driver has 1 dispute upheld in the last 90 days but 0 of them are route disputes, so the 'repeated route offence' condition for an account flag is not met on the route history alone.

weaknesses: The rider's own chat agreement (F8, at 10:01) preceded the off-route segment start (F3, 10:04), which is exactly the RD-5 'agreed before leaving the optimal route' pattern; the driver will use F7/F8 to argue the Halus Link routing was consented to and the segment is exempt.

The fare fact F4 shows the billed distance equals the optimal distance (9.9 km) and F6 shows no toll, waiting or manual add-on, so the driver/respondent will say the rider's complaint of 'I paid more than the estimate' is factually wrong for a fixed-price RydeX fare — the rider's loss is time (F2: +2.7 min), not money.

The traffic records (F10, F11: both band 4, 30–39 km/h) show real-mild slowdowns on the Tampines Expressway and Punggol Road during the trip, which the driver will use to argue a 'reasonable cause' for rerouting even though RD-4 requires an incident at band 1/2, not band 4.

claims.assertion: The only off-route segment (10:04–10:07, +1.73 km) was pre-arranged with the rider: the driver asked about diverting via Halus Link at 10:01 and the rider replied "Sure, go ahead" at 10:01, i.e. the rider's agreement timestamp precedes the segment's 10:04 start.

The diversion was not for personal convenience but was a rider-agreed alternative given building congestion - Tampines Expressway was recorded at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) across 09:49–10:21, covering the trip window.
The trip was a RydeX fixed-quote service, and the billed distance (9.9 km) did not exceed the optimal route (9.9 km), so no extra mileage was charged to the rider for the deviation.

The $23.32 total is fully accounted for by published components - base $3.90, distance $14.02, time $3.93, platform $1.47, no waiting fee, no surge (1.0x) and no discount - leaving no unpublished or overcharged item to refund.

The rider's own complaint is that she paid more than the estimate, but the fare fact shows the billed distance equals the quoted optimal distance, so on the fixed-quote model no recoverable amount can be computed from any fare or gps fact.

No account flag is warranted: the driver's 90-day dispute history shows 1 dispute with 0 route-deviation disputes upheld, so the "repeated route offender" condition for an account referral is not met.

weaknesses: RD-5 requires the agreement to precede the deviation, and the rider's consent (F8, 10:01) does precede the segment start (F3, 10:04) - but the rider may argue the consent covered only "traffic ahead on Tampines Expressway", while the segment ran up to 947 m from the optimal route (F3), which is a large detour to justify on a 1.73 km saving claim.

The diversion had no formal RD-4 justification: traffic facts show only band 4 (30–39 km/h) congestion (F10, F11), which is not the band 1–2 level RD-4(b) contemplates, and there were no traffic incidents at all (F12) - so the driver's "traffic was building up" statement (F9) cannot stand alone as a reasonable-cause exemption, and the segment's exemption rests entirely on the rider's consent under RD-5.

The driver drove 11.7 km against a 9.9 km optimal route (+18%) and 17.8 min against a 15 min estimate (F1, F2), which will be used to argue the deviation was objectively substantial even if it was free of charge on a fixed quote.

F14 shows the rider has 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, which the rider's side may use to argue she is dispute-prone, but it equally cuts against the driver's request for a flag_account and must not be treated as deciding this case.

points.response: Conceded on consent timing: the rider's "Sure, go ahead" (F8, 10:01) does precede the off-route segment start of 10:04 (F3), so that segment is exempt under RD-5 and I withdraw my C3/consent argument. What is not resolved by consent is the remainder of the driven route: the GPS shows 11.7 km against a 9.9 km optimal route (F1), i.e. 1.8 km beyond the compliant route of which only 1.73 km belongs to the one segment F3 identifies.

Band 4 at 30–39 km/h (F10, F11) is neither a DataMall incident nor a band 1/2 record, and F12 confirms no incidents at all, so RD-4(b) explicitly does not grant a standalone exemption at this level; the driver's own statement (F9) cannot substitute for the traffic evidence RD-4 requires.

Accepted: the fare fact shows the billed distance equals the optimal distance (F4) inside a total of $23.32 (F6), so on this fixed-quote RydeX trip the extra 1.8 km driven in F1 produced no mileage charge — my case does not rest on a fare excess that does not exist.

The component list is not disputed, but it shows no charge traceable to the deviation: waiting $0.00, no ERP/toll item, no manual add-on (F6), so under RD-2's non-metered branch the refundable amount computes to $0 even though the driver's breach of the shortest-route duty under RD-1 is recorded.

Conceded in substance: no recoverable amount can be computed from any fare or GPS fact for this fixed-quote trip (F4, F6), so I no longer seek money for the deviation. The rider's remaining remedy is the recording of the RD-1 violation and the platform-level consequence of a driver who drove 11.7 km on a 9.9 km route without answering advance disclosure of routing options beyond the one stated.

Agreed there is no basis for flag_account against this driver — F15 shows 0 route disputes upheld in 90 days — but that cuts both ways: the absence of a reference flag does not erase the RD-1 breach found in F3 and F1.
I withdraw my own claim C3: the consent timing (F8 at 10:01 before F3's 10:04) does exempt that segment under RD-5, and I will not argue the rider's agreement was narrower than the route driven.

I restate C5 with the clause the respondent himself invokes: RD-2's non-metered branch yields a $0 refundable amount (computed from the billed fare F6, which contains no off-route ERP/toll or manual item), so the correct monetary outcome is no_action combined with a recorded RD-1 breach on the 1.8 km excess in F1.

The 1.73 km off-route segment exists (F3), but RD-1 exempts any segment excused by RD-3/RD-5, and this segment is exactly the rider-requested-and-agreed Halus Link routing, so it is not an "unexempted" segment under RD-1.

We do not rely on RD-4 for exemption; the segment is exempt under RD-5 because the driver raised the Halus Link route at 10:01 and the rider agreed at 10:01, before the segment started at 10:04, and the band 4 records on the Tampines Expressway only corroborate why the driver proposed it.
The rider's own concession that consent came in advance of the segment (F8 vs F3) confirms the RD-5 pattern, so the only surviving segment is exempt and no refundable mileage exists.
We agree the trip was a fixed-quote RydeX service billed at the optimal 9.9 km with no distance excess, no waiting fee and no undisclosed add-on (F4, F5, F6), so FARE-1 yields nothing to refund.

We accept the $0 monetary outcome (F4, F6), but record that the deviation itself must not be logged as an RD-1 breach: the segment is exempt under RD-5 (F7, F8, F3), and the note on D1-D6 stays on the record.

There is no basis for flag_account: the rider's route-upheld count is 0 (F14) and the driver's single upheld dispute is not a route dispute (F15), so RD-6's precondition of an upheld route dispute in this case plus a prior one is not met.

Kept: the fixed-quote structure of the RydeX fare (F4-F6) is what forecloses any money back, and the rider's complaint of paying more than the estimate is therefore factually mistaken on the fare facts.
The rider has now joined us in conceding no account flag is warranted, so D6 stands uncontested.
